## Key Solutions for Clean URLs After Authentication

### Silent Check-SSO (Recommended for SPAs)
You can configure a silent check-sso option. With this feature enabled, your browser will not perform a full redirect to the Keycloak server and back to your application, but this action will be performed in a hidden iframe. Therefore, your application resources are only loaded and parsed once by the browser, namely when the application is initialized and not again after the redirect back from Keycloak to your application.

This approach is particularly useful in case of SPAs (Single Page Applications). To enable the silent check-sso, you provide a silentCheckSsoRedirectUri attribute in the init method.

### Token Persistence Approaches
When using keycloak-js, the tokens (accessToken, refreshToken, and idToken) are stored in memory by default. That means when your app reloads, those tokens vanish. Keycloak sees you as unauthenticated and kicks off a new login flow. You can fix this by saving tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage after login, and restoring them on page load.

### Backend-Based Solution (Most Secure)
For the most secure solution, store tokens in HttpOnly cookies using your backend (e.g., Django, Node.js, etc.). JavaScript can't access HttpOnly cookies (safe from XSS). Tokens are attached to requests via cookies automatically. Ideal for enterprise-grade apps.

### Browser Limitations
Some browsers block third-party cookies by default — this can break silent SSO if Keycloak is hosted on a different domain.

The silent check-sso method is generally the cleanest solution for SPAs as it avoids visible redirect loops while maintaining security.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about Keycloak-JS responseMode configuration and its interaction with SPA frameworks like Vue Router:

## ResponseMode: Fragment vs Query

The responseMode parameter sets the OpenID Connect response mode sent to Keycloak server at login request, with valid values being query or fragment. The default value is fragment, which means that after successful authentication Keycloak will redirect to JavaScript application with OpenID Connect parameters added in URL fragment, and this is generally safer and recommended over query.

## Hash Cleanup Issues with SPAs

However, there's a known issue with hash/fragment cleanup in SPA applications: Users see the entire hash in the browser address bar even when specifying history mode (not hash mode), which is not in compliance with RFC 6749. With Vue 3, fragments are being left behind on the URL in the user's address bar.

## SPA Router Integration Problems

During auth handling, Keycloak JS SDK removes the hash from the URL, but the problem is that frameworks like SvelteKit restore the hash after the load function and the rendered URL has the auth redirect hash visible. It's common for SPA applications to use hash-based routing, but the only safe way to use keycloak-js is to initialize before any router behavior.

## Key Recommendations

The silent check-sso approach is particularly useful in case of SPAs (Single Page Applications), which can help mitigate some of these hash cleanup issues by performing authentication in a hidden iframe rather than with full redirects.

# Keycloak JavaScript Adapter: ResponseMode, URL Handling, and SPA Configuration

## ResponseMode

The documentation defines responseMode as the "OpenID Connect response mode send to Keycloak server at login request." Valid values are `query` or `fragment`, with `fragment` as the default. The docs note that fragment mode is "generally safer and recommended over `query`."

```javascript
await keycloak.init({
    responseMode: 'fragment' // default, recommended
});
```

## URL Cleanup After Redirect

The documentation explicitly warns: "Because initializing the adapter can cause mutations to the URL of the page, make sure that the adapter is **always** initialized before initializing a router of your client-side framework."

This addresses hash fragment management—by initializing Keycloak first, you prevent routing conflicts when parameters are added to the URL during authentication.

## Silent Check-SSO for SPAs

For Single Page Applications, the docs recommend the silent `check-sso` feature, which performs authentication checks "in a hidden iframe" rather than full page redirects. This ensures "your application resources are only loaded and parsed once by the browser."

```javascript
await keycloak.init({
    onLoad: 'check-sso',
    silentCheckSsoRedirectUri: `${location.origin}/silent-check-sso.html`
});
```

The silent check-sso redirect URI must be a simple HTML file that posts received tokens back to the main application via `parent.postMessage()`.

**Note:** Silent check-sso functionality is limited in modern browsers with tracking protection enabled.

# Keycloak URL Fragment Issue: Summary

## The Exact Issue
After successful login with keycloak-js in Vue 3 applications, URL fragments containing authentication parameters remain visible in the browser's address bar, violating RFC 6749 security standards.

Example problematic URL:
```
http://localhost:9000/home/#state=3cedca45-59cc-43e2-aadc-88c07a14dca2&session_state=...&code=...
```

## Root Cause
The issue stems from an interaction between keycloak-js and vue-router module initialization. Vue-router captures `window.location` during its import phase, before keycloak-js can remove fragments. When `app.use(router)` executes later, vue-router reintroduces the fragments through its history navigation logic.

As one developer noted: "The module init for vue-router is capturing a value from `window.location` and using it later for routing before the caller executes app.use(router)."

## Recommended Solutions

**1. Initialize Keycloak Before Router Import**
Load keycloak-js in a separate script tag before your application's main module:

```html
<script src="/kc/js/keycloak.js"></script>
<script>
  window.keycloak = new Keycloak({...});
  window.kc_init = keycloak.init({...});
</script>
<script type="module" src="/src/main.js"></script>
```

Then await in main.js before importing router.

**2. Use Query Response Mode**
Configure keycloak to use query parameters instead of fragments:
```js
initOption: { responseMode: 'query' }
```

**3. Silent Check-SSO**
Implement `silentCheckSsoRedirectUri` to redirect authentication parameters to a silent callback page rather than the main application URL.

Here is my analysis and the recommended solution.

---

## Root Cause

This is a well-documented issue tracked in [keycloak/keycloak#14742](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/14742). The problem is a **race condition between vue-router's module initialization and keycloak-js URL cleanup**.

Here is what happens step-by-step in your current code:

1. In `main.ts`, you `import router from './router'` at the **top level** (line 6).
2. This import is hoisted by the JavaScript module system. It executes **immediately** when the module loads -- before `initAuth()` is called.
3. When `router.ts` runs, `createRouter({ history: createWebHistory() })` is called. At this point, `createWebHistory()` captures `window.location` (including the hash fragment) and stores it internally.
4. Later, `initAuth()` runs, keycloak-js processes the redirect, and your `finally` block cleans the URL with `history.replaceState`.
5. But it is too late -- vue-router already captured the original URL with the hash fragment. When `app.use(router)` runs, vue-router performs its initial navigation based on the captured URL, **restoring the hash fragment** back into the address bar.

Your `responseMode: 'query'` setting and `history.replaceState` cleanup are both correct in isolation, but they cannot win against vue-router re-applying the captured URL.

## Recommended Solution

The fix is to ensure Keycloak finishes its init (and URL cleanup) **before** vue-router is ever imported. You need to use a **dynamic import** for the router so it is not loaded until after authentication completes.

### Changes to `main.ts`

```typescript
import { createApp } from 'vue'
import Toast from 'vue-toastification'
import 'vue-toastification/dist/index.css'
import './style.css'
import App from './App.vue'
import { initAuth } from './auth'

initAuth().then(async (authenticated) => {
  if (authenticated) {
    // Dynamic import: router module is loaded AFTER keycloak has cleaned the URL
    const { default: router } = await import('./router')
    
    const app = createApp(App)
    app.use(router)
    app.use(Toast, {
      position: 'top-right',
      timeout: 4000,
      closeOnClick: true,
      pauseOnHover: true,
    })
    app.mount('#app')
  }
})
```

The key change is replacing the static `import router from './router'` at the top of the file with `await import('./router')` inside the `.then()` callback. This guarantees that `createWebHistory()` runs only after keycloak-js has already processed the redirect callback and your `finally` block has cleaned the URL.

### Changes to `auth.ts` (minor cleanup)

Your `auth.ts` is mostly fine. The `finally` block URL cleanup is good defensive coding. However, with `responseMode: 'query'`, Keycloak puts params in the query string, not the hash. So the `url.hash = ''` line is targeting the wrong thing if the hash is actually being set by Keycloak's default `fragment` mode leaking through. You could simplify the cleanup to be more thorough:

```typescript
export async function initAuth(): Promise<boolean> {
  let authenticated = false
  try {
    authenticated = await keycloak.init({
      onLoad: 'login-required',
      checkLoginIframe: false,
      responseMode: 'query',
    })
  } finally {
    // Clean any leftover Keycloak params from URL
    const url = new URL(window.location.href)
    const keycloakParams = ['state', 'session_state', 'code', 'iss']
    keycloakParams.forEach((p) => url.searchParams.delete(p))
    url.hash = ''
    window.history.replaceState(null, '', url.pathname + url.search)
  }

  // ... rest unchanged
}
```

This part is already correct in your code. The real fix is the dynamic import in `main.ts`.

---

## Why Other Approaches Fall Short

| Approach | Problem |
|---|---|
| `responseMode: 'query'` alone | Does not help because vue-router still captures the URL before cleanup happens |
| `history.replaceState` in `finally` | Vue-router re-applies its captured URL, overwriting your cleanup |
| `silentCheckSsoRedirectUri` | Only works with `check-sso`, not `login-required`; also requires a separate HTML file and has issues with browsers that block third-party cookies |

## Summary

The one-line fix is: **dynamically import the router module after Keycloak init completes**. Change `import router from './router'` to `const { default: router } = await import('./router')` inside the post-authentication callback. This ensures `createWebHistory()` never sees the dirty URL.

This is the solution recommended in the [keycloak/keycloak#14742](https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/14742) GitHub issue discussion and aligns with the [official Keycloak JS adapter documentation](https://www.keycloak.org/securing-apps/javascript-adapter), which states:

> "Because initializing the adapter can cause mutations to the URL of the page, make sure that the adapter is **always** initialized before initializing a router of your client-side framework."
